title: Stream Processing Engines Compared
summary: Micro-batch and true per-event engines make a fundamentally different trade between latency, throughput, and fault-tolerance cost. Learn which shape a given latency target actually requires.

slides.markdown:
Every engine that processes [Kafka](kafka-deep-dive)-style streams makes one foundational architectural choice early: does it process events one at a time as they arrive, or does it slice the stream into small batches and process each slice? That choice — micro-batch vs true per-event — determines the engine's latency floor, its throughput ceiling, and how it recovers from a failure.

Neither model is strictly better. This topic covers the trade-off precisely enough that you can look at a latency requirement and know which model it actually needs, rather than defaulting to whichever engine is trendiest.

The two dominant execution models differ in the fundamental unit of work:

| | Micro-batch | True per-event (continuous) |
|---|---|---|
| Unit of work | A small batch of events accumulated over a fixed interval | One event at a time |
| Latency floor | At least one batch interval (commonly ~100ms-1s) | Sub-millisecond to low-milliseconds possible |
| Fault recovery | Rerun the failed micro-batch | Checkpoint and resume mid-stream (finer-grained) |
| Familiar model | Feels like repeatedly running a small batch job | A continuously running pipeline with no batch boundary |

Both are legitimate ways to implement everything covered earlier in this group — windowing, watermarks, state — the difference is entirely in *how often* work gets grouped and how failure recovery is scoped, not in what results are computable.

slides.subTitle: Batches of the stream on a fixed interval
slides.markdown:
A **micro-batch** engine collects incoming events for a short, fixed interval — say, 500ms — then runs its processing logic once over that whole batch, much like a small, repeated batch job. The next interval's events accumulate while the current batch is processing.

This has a real practical upside: because each unit of work is a small, self-contained batch, the same fault-tolerance and optimization machinery that a batch engine already has (retry a failed task, optimize a query plan) applies directly — you're not building a fundamentally new execution engine, you're running a batch engine very frequently. This is exactly why frameworks with mature batch engines (Spark's execution model, covered in [Spark Architecture](spark-architecture)) extended naturally into streaming via micro-batching.

The cost is the interval itself: no result can ever be faster than one batch interval, because the engine genuinely hasn't looked at that data until the batch containing it runs.

slides.subTitle: Lower latency floor, different fault-tolerance cost
slides.markdown:
A **true per-event** (continuous) engine processes each record as it arrives, with no batch boundary at all — there's no "wait for the interval" step, so the latency floor drops to whatever the processing logic itself takes, often single-digit milliseconds or less.

The fault-tolerance model has to work differently, though: since there's no natural batch boundary to retry, recovery relies on the checkpointing mechanism covered in [Stateful Stream Processing](stateful-stream-processing) — snapshotting state and resuming mid-stream from an exact offset, rather than "just rerun the failed batch." That's a more sophisticated (and historically harder-to-implement-correctly) recovery model than micro-batch's "rerun this small unit," which is part of why continuous engines took longer to mature to production-grade fault tolerance than micro-batch ones did.

The pay-off is real when latency genuinely matters: fraud detection, real-time bidding, and anything with a latency budget under a few hundred milliseconds usually needs this model, because micro-batch's interval floor is often already too slow on its own.

Orthogonal to micro-batch vs per-event is a second, separate choice: does the stream-processing logic run as its own dedicated cluster, or is it a **library embedded directly inside an application**?

A dedicated cluster (a standalone deployment of the processing engine) is the standard choice when the processing is substantial, shared across teams, or needs the engine's own resource management and scaling independent of any one application. A library-embedded approach runs the processing logic inside the same process as the application that owns it — no separate cluster to operate, tighter integration with application code and its own state, at the cost of scaling only as far as that one application can, and no shared processing infrastructure across teams.

The choice tracks organizational shape as much as technical need: a platform team serving many consumers usually wants a dedicated cluster; a single service team with a narrow, self-contained streaming need inside one application sometimes finds embedding cheaper to operate than standing up and maintaining a separate cluster.

Putting rough numbers on the trade-off makes it concrete:

| | Micro-batch | Per-event (continuous) |
|---|---|---|
| Typical latency floor | ~100ms-2s (tied to batch interval) | Single-digit ms to low tens of ms |
| Peak throughput per node | Often higher — batching amortizes per-record overhead | Often lower per node — per-record overhead paid individually, though modern engines close much of this gap |
| Best fit | High-throughput aggregation where sub-second latency isn't required | Latency-critical paths where every millisecond of the batch interval is a real cost |

The throughput gap between the two models has narrowed considerably as continuous engines have matured — it's a much smaller factor today than it was a decade ago. The latency floor gap, however, is closer to fundamental: a micro-batch engine cannot beat its own interval, no matter how well-optimized, because it genuinely hasn't started processing an event until its batch begins.

slides.sectionTitle: Reaching for the lowest-latency engine unnecessarily
slides.markdown:
A team builds a nightly-refresh dashboard — data only needs to be accurate as of "sometime this morning" — but picks the lowest-latency continuous streaming engine available, because "real-time" sounds more impressive than a scheduled job.

The cost isn't hypothetical: continuous engines generally carry more operational complexity than a scheduled batch job (always-on infrastructure, more subtle failure modes, checkpoint tuning) for a workload that a batch job running once every few hours would have solved with a fraction of the operational surface area and cost.

The question to ask before reaching for streaming at all: what's the actual latency budget, stated in a number, and does anything downstream break if that number is minutes or hours instead of milliseconds? If nothing breaks, the scheduled batch model is very often the simpler, cheaper, equally-correct answer — streaming should be a response to a real latency requirement, not a default architectural preference.

Beyond raw latency and throughput, the right engine choice often comes down to **ecosystem fit** — what you get for free by staying inside a framework you already use:

- **Shared batch-and-stream code** — a framework whose batch and streaming APIs share the same programming model (as with [Spark's](spark-architecture) DataFrame API spanning both) lets a team write similar logic once and reuse skills and tooling across both workloads, at some cost to how far either mode can be optimized versus a purpose-built engine.
- **Lowest possible latency** — a purpose-built continuous engine, chosen specifically because nothing else hits the latency target, even if it means learning a separate framework and operating a separate cluster.
- **Embedding in a service** — a lightweight, library-embedded option chosen because the processing logic needs to live inside one application's process, not a standalone cluster.

None of these is universally correct; the right answer follows from which of the three actually matters most for your team's constraints — existing skills and infrastructure, a hard latency number, or a deployment shape that rules out a separate cluster.

Put the whole topic together on one concrete decision: a team needs fraud scoring on payment events with a **p99 latency budget under 150ms**, running inside an existing payments service that already has its own deployment pipeline.

Walking the trade-offs: the latency budget alone rules out micro-batch — even a fast 100ms batch interval eats most of the budget before any processing happens, leaving no margin. That points to a true per-event engine. The "inside an existing service" constraint then points toward a library-embedded option over standing up a dedicated cluster, since the team doesn't want to operate separate infrastructure for one latency-critical path.

The answer that falls out — a per-event, library-embedded engine — wasn't chosen because it's the newest or fastest option in the abstract; it's the one that satisfies both the hard latency number and the deployment constraint simultaneously. That's the reasoning pattern to reuse, not the specific engine.

Engine choice is the *implementation* decision; the next topic, Streaming Architecture Patterns — Lambda & Kappa, is the *system architecture* decision one level up — how batch and streaming pipelines combine at the organizational and data-flow level, independent of which specific engine runs the streaming half.

The two connect directly: Kappa architecture's core bet — a single streaming pipeline can also handle reprocessing history — depends on having an engine (and a log with enough retention) fast and cheap enough to replay large volumes without the operational cost this topic just walked through for the wrong workload.
